transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, well, I came in because I've been having these... these really awful, unwanted thoughts. It really started when I was working on my aunt’s memorial piece recently. I'm an artist, I actually got my degree in illustration, so my family usually asks me to handle the creative stuff for things like this. Which is fine, I don't mind, though honestly getting good archival materials right now is so frustrating. I had to go to three different stores just to find the right acid-free matting because everything online takes weeks to ship and the local places are always out of stock. 

But anyway, while I was working on her piece, I just kept getting these thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like, if I made one wrong photo placement or picked the wrong color, it would mean I didn’t love her enough. And I couldn’t just brush them off like normal creative doubts, you know? It felt so heavy. She was always so supportive of my art, too—she used to buy me those little paint-by-numbers kits when I was like, six, the ones with the horses? I was completely obsessed with horses back then. But yeah, those thoughts about ruining her memorial just wouldn't stop, and I couldn't just work through it like I usually do.
Did these thoughts about dishonoring your aunt feel like they were coming from outside of yourself, or did they feel like your own thoughts?

No, they... they were definitely my own thoughts. I knew it was just my brain coming up with it, it wasn't like a voice from outside or anything. It’s just that they were these really awful, unwanted thoughts, you know? 

Like I was saying, it was my own mind telling me that if I made one wrong photo placement or color choice, it meant I didn't love her enough. Which is so frustrating because usually I can just brush off creative doubts. Like, if I'm debating between using a cerulean blue or an ultramarine—which actually makes a massive difference if you're trying to mix a clean purple, because cerulean leans way too yellow-green and you just end up with mud. I spent like three weeks in my sophomore year of college just doing color theory swatches. My professor was incredibly strict about it, he used to make us start completely over if the value was even slightly off. 

But... wait, sorry, what was I saying? Right, normally I just move past the doubt. But these thoughts about dishonoring her were definitely mine, they were just so heavy that I couldn't brush them off like I usually do.
Have these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt continued to bother you since you finished working on her memorial piece?

Well, yeah, they actually have. Even after I finished it and handed it over to my uncle. He decided to put it in this really gorgeous oak frame, which was a huge relief because I was so worried he’d pick something metallic. Metallic frames can look so cheap unless you get them custom-made at a proper gallery, and even then, they reflect way too much glare if they aren't matte. We actually had this massive debate in my senior exhibition class about framing—my friend Sarah spent like four hundred dollars on this brushed nickel frame that completely distracted from her watercolor pieces. Watercolors are already so delicate, you know? You really have to let the paper breathe, especially if you're using cold-pressed, otherwise the texture gets totally lost behind the glass. 

But... wait, sorry, what was I talking about? Oh, the memorial piece. Right. Yeah, even though it's completely finished and the service is over, I still get those exact same awful thoughts. Like, out of nowhere, my brain will just tell me I dishonored her, or that picking that one specific photo instead of another meant I didn't care about her enough. I still can't just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. It just keeps bothering me.
Are these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt affecting your ability to do other things you normally enjoy or need to do?

Yeah, it is. I mean, I’m still getting most of my work done, thankfully. But it takes me so much longer now. Like, the extra time I lose in the studio because I'm just stuck in my head... it actually cost me a grant deadline recently. 

Which, honestly, grants are so incredibly competitive right now anyway. I was applying for this one from the state arts council, and their online portal is just a complete nightmare. You have to upload everything as a specific PDF size, and if your portfolio images are even a fraction of a megabyte over, the whole system just crashes and deletes all your progress. My friend Mark was applying for the exact same one—he does these massive resin pours, which honestly I think are a bit of a fad right now, but they do sell really well at summer street fairs. He actually spilled a whole gallon of industrial epoxy on his studio floor last month and had to scrape it up with a heat gun. He said the fumes were just awful, you really need proper ventilation for that kind of medium. 

But... wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, if the thoughts are affecting my life. Yeah. So missing that grant deadline really sucked. And because I've been losing so much time in the studio dealing with this, I also had to back out of a gallery talk that I had actually really wanted to do. Which is a huge shame because I bought a really gorgeous linen blazer specifically for that talk. Linen wrinkles so fast though, you basically can't even sit down in it if you want to look presentable... but yeah, it's definitely getting in the way of things I need to do.
Do you find yourself repeatedly thinking about these unwanted thoughts throughout the day, even when you're not actively trying to think about them?

Yeah, all the time. It's like... even when I'm just trying to make breakfast or run errands, those exact same thoughts just pop up. I'll just be standing there and suddenly my brain is like, *you dishonored her, you didn't love her enough because you picked the wrong photo or the wrong color.* And I'm not even trying to think about the memorial piece! 

It's actually a lot like when I get a song stuck in my head, but way worse. Last week I had that one Fleetwood Mac song stuck in my head for like three days straight. You know, "Dreams"? It's a great song, obviously, Stevie Nicks is an absolute icon. My mom actually saw them live on the Rumours tour in '77. She said Lindsey Buckingham broke a guitar string right in the middle of a solo and just kept playing like nothing happened. She kept the ticket stub in this little scrapbook for years until our basement flooded back in 2015. We lost so many good photo albums in that flood, which is probably why I'm so paranoid about archival quality now. I only use acid-free sleeves for my prints, because otherwise they yellow so fast. 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? What were we talking about? Oh, right, the thoughts. Yeah, they just keep coming back all day long, completely on their own. I really wish I could just brush them off like my normal creative doubts, but I just... can't. They just won't leave me alone.
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over to try to make these unwanted thoughts go away?

Yeah, I do. It's really frustrating actually. Whenever those thoughts hit, I feel like I have to go back and check the memorial piece, or at least the digital files and layout photos of it. I'll end up rereading the label text, nudging the same objects on my drafting table, and just checking those layout photos over and over again. I have to keep doing it until it finally feels... I don't know, 'settled.' 

It's kind of like when I'm setting up a still life for a charcoal study. You know, you move the drapery just a fraction of an inch, and then you step back, and the lighting is completely different. Charcoal is so unforgiving with light. I actually switched to vine charcoal recently because compressed charcoal just gets everywhere. My studio mate, Jessica, she uses compressed charcoal and she literally has black fingerprints all over her coffee mugs. It drives me insane. She drinks this really weird herbal tea, too—like, licorice root and peppermint? The smell is just overpowering. I keep telling her she needs to switch to a travel mug with a lid if she's going to drink that in the studio, especially with all the charcoal dust floating around. 

But... wait. I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought again. What was I saying? Oh, right, doing things over and over. Yeah, I just keep checking the layout photos and adjusting things on my table until that awful feeling goes away. Even though part of me knows it’s already completely fine and I’m just losing precious studio time doing it.
When you're checking the memorial piece over and over, are you trying to prevent something bad from happening?

No, not really... I'm not worried about like, a curse or bad luck or anything happening to me or my family. It's more about just needing that feeling of it being right. I just have to keep rereading the label text I wrote for her, and nudging the objects on my drafting table, and checking those layout photos over and over again until it finally feels 'settled' in my chest. 

Which is so weird because I know, logically, that the piece is fine. It's actually a really beautiful tribute. I used this gorgeous handmade paper from Japan for the backing—Washi paper, I think it's called? It has these tiny little flecks of gold leaf pressed right into the fibers. I had to order it from this specialty shop in San Francisco because the art supply stores around here just carry the mass-produced stuff. The shipping took forever, too, because they used FedEx Ground and the driver just left it on my porch in the rain without even ringing the bell. Thank god the shop owner wrapped it in plastic first, or the whole sheet would have been ruined. Water damage on paper is basically impossible to fix, especially if it's not sized properly. You get these awful tide lines that just ruin the whole aesthetic. 

Wait, sorry... I got distracted again. What did you ask? Oh, right, preventing something bad. No, I'm not trying to stop something from happening. I just... I know I'm wasting so much studio time doing it, but I just can't stop checking and nudging things until that uneasy feeling goes away and it finally feels settled.
Do you feel less anxious after checking the memorial piece and making adjustments?

Yeah, it does help. Like I was saying a minute ago, I'll just end up rereading the label text, nudging the exact same objects on my table, and checking those layout photos over and over. And once I finally do all that, the anxiety does drop. It finally feels 'settled.' Even though, like I said, part of me knows the piece is already completely fine and I’m just losing precious studio time doing all this. 

Which actually reminds me, I lost so much studio time yesterday because the radiator in my building completely broke. It was freezing in there. You really can't work with cold hands, especially not when you're trying to do delicate paper cutting. I have this really nice precision craft knife—it has this ergonomic padded grip, which is a total lifesaver because I used to get awful calluses on my index finger. My friend Mark, he does linocut printing, and his hands are just completely wrecked from his carving tools. He won't wear gloves because he says it ruins his tactile feedback, but then he gets this black block printing ink under his nails that literally stays there for weeks. It looks terrible when we go out for dinner. We went to this new Italian place last week and the waiter kept staring at his hands... 

Wait, I'm so sorry. I'm rambling again, aren't I? You asked if I feel less anxious. Yes, doing the checking and the nudging definitely makes that awful anxious feeling go away, at least for a little while.
Do you think checking the memorial piece over and over helps reduce your anxiety?

Yeah, it really does. I know I've said it like three times now, but I'll end up rereading the label text I wrote, nudging the exact same objects on my table, and checking those layout photos over and over again. And when I do that, the anxiety definitely goes down. It finally just feels 'settled.' Even though, like I keep saying, part of me knows the piece is already completely fine and I’m just losing precious studio time doing it. 

Which is so frustrating because I have a deadline coming up for this local gallery showcase. They're doing this whole exhibition on grief and memory, which is perfect for the memorial piece, but the gallery director is so disorganized. His name is David, and he literally sends emails at 2:00 AM with these frantic subject lines in all caps. And he always uses way too many exclamation points. It's like, David, I am trying to sleep, I don't need an emergency email about the hors d'oeuvres menu for the opening night. He wants to serve these weird little smoked salmon blinis, but I told him my friend Jessica—the one with the compressed charcoal problem—is deathly allergic to fish. Like, throat-closing-up allergic. She carries two EpiPens in her bag at all times. Her bag is this really beautiful vintage leather satchel she found at a flea market in Portland... 

Oh, gosh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so sorry. You were asking if it helps reduce the anxiety. Yes, rereading the text and nudging things on my table and checking the photos definitely makes the anxiety go away. It just wastes so much time.
Do you feel like you're trying to make things perfectly symmetrical or exact when you're checking and nudging the objects on your table?

Not exactly symmetry, no. I know I sound like a broken record here, repeating the exact same thing about how I just keep rereading the label text and checking those layout photos and nudging the stuff on my table over and over. But it's really just about getting that 'settled' feeling, not making it perfectly even or measured. Even though I know the piece is completely fine and I'm just burning through my studio time doing it. 

I actually don't even use a ruler when I'm placing the objects. Which is funny because I have this gorgeous solid brass ruler that I bought at an antique market in Seattle. It’s so heavy, it basically doubles as a paperweight. My cat, Barnaby, is always trying to knock things off my desk, and he actually managed to push that heavy brass ruler off the edge last week. It put a huge dent in the hardwood floor. My landlord is going to be furious when I move out. He's already so paranoid about the floors because he just had them refinished right before I signed the lease, and he made me put these little adhesive felt pads on every single piece of furniture. I had to go to Home Depot and buy three packs of them, and the guy at the checkout was so incredibly slow. He kept trying to talk to me about his own woodworking projects, which, like, is fine, but I was double-parked...

Oh, gosh, I did it again. I'm sorry, I keep drifting off today. But yeah, to answer your question, it’s not about making things perfectly symmetrical or exact. I just keep nudging those same objects around until it finally feels settled.
Do you feel like you're trying to control something when you're checking and nudging the objects on your table?

Control? Um, I don't know if it's about control, exactly. I know I'm basically just repeating the exact same sentence at this point, but I really just end up rereading the label text, nudging the same objects on the table, and checking those layout photos over and over until it finally feels 'settled.' Even though, like I keep saying, part of me knows the piece is already completely fine and I’m just losing precious studio time doing it. It doesn't feel like a power trip or anything, just a feeling I need to fix.

Speaking of control, though, my old sculpture professor in college was the biggest control freak I've ever met in my life. Professor Aris. He literally wouldn't let us use anything but this one specific brand of imported German armature wire. It was ridiculously expensive, and you could only buy it at this one tiny, cramped art supply store downtown. The owner of that store was this grumpy guy named Stan who always had a half-chewed cigar in his mouth, which is insane because you are definitely not supposed to smoke around turpentine and oil solvents. He actually yelled at me once because my backpack bumped into a display of kneaded erasers and knocked them all over the floor. Kneaded erasers pick up dust instantly, so they were basically ruined, and he made me pay for like twenty of them. I ended up giving a bunch of them to my niece for her birthday, along with this huge set of sparkly gel pens. She's really into drawing horses right now, but she draws their legs so long they look like spiders... 

Oh my gosh, I am so sorry. I am totally off track again. What were we talking about? Right, control. No, I don't think I'm trying to control anything when I'm nudging the objects around. I just have to keep doing it until that unsettled feeling goes away, even though it wastes so much of my day.
Is there something specific that you are afraid will happen if you don't check and nudge the objects on your table?

Yeah, actually, there is. That's kind of the main reason I came in, honestly. When I started working on my aunt's memorial piece, I just kept getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like, if I made one wrong photo placement or picked the wrong color choice, it would mean I didn't love her enough. 

And color is so tricky, you know? Her favorite color was this very specific shade of marigold yellow. She used to wear this marigold knit cardigan all the time when I was a kid. She bought it on a trip to Santa Fe, I think. She absolutely loved the desert. She always said the dry heat was better for her joints. My joints have actually been aching a bit lately, mostly my wrists from sculpting and wedging clay. I tried wearing one of those copper compression gloves while I work, but it smelled so heavily of neoprene, kind of like a wetsuit. I wore a wetsuit once when I went snorkeling in the Keys, and the tour guide was this guy named Todd who was completely obsessed with pointing out manatees. He kept stopping the boat every five minutes to look at them, and we ended up getting completely sunburned because we were out on the water for like four hours... 

Oh my gosh, I am doing it again. I am so sorry. Manatees. Really? I don't know how my brain just takes off like that. 

But um, what was I saying? Right, the memorial piece. Yeah, I just couldn't brush those thoughts off like normal creative doubts. It's this overwhelming fear that if I don't check the photos and nudge everything until it's right, I'm basically proving I didn't care about her.
What exactly do you think will happen if you don't check and nudge the objects on your table?

I mean, like I was saying, it's really just that awful feeling that I'm going to dishonor her memory. That if I don't get it perfectly settled, it proves I didn't love her enough. It's not like I think the ceiling is going to cave in or something, it's just... this heavy guilt about the memorial piece. 

Which is so frustrating because I really wanted this piece to be beautiful, you know? I was even thinking about incorporating some dried flowers into the resin. I went to this amazing botanical garden last weekend to get some inspiration, and they had this incredible greenhouse full of orchids. It was so humid in there, my hair completely frizzed out. I have this curly hair that just absorbs moisture like a sponge. I've tried like a dozen different serums, and the only one that kind of works is this imported Moroccan oil, but the bottle leaks everywhere. It ruined my favorite canvas tote bag. The tote bag had this really cool screen print of a vintage bicycle on it. I bought it at a farmer's market from this girl who was selling handmade soaps too. The soap smelled like lavender and oatmeal, which sounds nice, but it actually made my skin break out in hives. I had to take Benadryl for three days and I was so sleepy I barely got any work done...

Ugh, I'm doing it again. I'm sorry. I really need to focus. But yeah, to answer your question, there's no specific disaster I think will happen. It's just that overwhelming fear of disrespecting my aunt if I don't do the checking and nudging until it feels right.
Do you feel like you're trying to make the memorial piece perfect when you're checking and nudging the objects on your table?

Perfect? Um, I don't really know if I'd use the word perfect. I mean, art is never really perfect anyway, you know? It's so subjective. Like, I went to this gallery opening downtown a couple of weeks ago, and the featured artist had these massive canvases that were just painted entirely beige. Just flat, boring beige. And people were standing around drinking cheap wine acting like it was the most brilliant, perfect masterpiece they'd ever seen. 

The wine they served was actually terrible, by the way. It gave me this instant headache. I usually only drink white wine, specifically this one Pinot Grigio from Oregon, because my roommate in college, Sarah, was from Portland and she got me hooked on it. Sarah actually moved to Seattle recently to work for some big tech company, which is so weird because she was a theater major. She used to put on these wild avant-garde plays in our dorm basement where the actors would basically just scream at the audience for twenty minutes straight... 

Oh my god, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry. I don't know why I keep drifting off like that today. My brain is just all over the place. 

But um, to answer your question, no, I don't think I'm trying to make the memorial piece perfect. It's not about making it look flawless or anything like that. Like I said before, it's really just about doing the nudging and checking until that horrible unsettled feeling goes away.
Do you feel like you would be able to stop checking and nudging the objects if someone you trusted told you that the memorial piece was fine as it is?

I don't think so, honestly. Even if someone I really trust told me it was fine, I'd probably still do it. Like, part of me already knows it's fine, you know? I know I'm just losing studio time. But I still end up rereading the label text, nudging the same objects on the table, and checking the layout photos over and over until it feels "settled." 

It's kind of like when my sister tells me an outfit looks good, but I still change three times before we go out. She has this incredible fashion sense, though. She works as a buyer for this boutique downtown that sells a lot of sustainable clothing. They have these really beautiful linen dresses, but they wrinkle if you even just look at them wrong. I bought one for a summer wedding last year—it was an outdoor wedding at this gorgeous vineyard. The wine was actually fantastic, not like that gallery opening I was talking about. But the bugs at the vineyard were awful. I got bit by a mosquito right on my eyelid and it swelled up so much I looked like I'd been in a boxing match. I had to wear my sunglasses the entire reception, even after the sun went down, which made me look like one of those pretentious celebrities trying to hide from the paparazzi...

Sorry, I'm doing it again. The tangents, I mean. But yeah, no, someone telling me the piece is fine wouldn't stop me. I just have to keep doing the checking and nudging until that specific unsettled feeling goes away, even though I know it's a waste of time.
Do you think you would feel less anxious if you were able to accept that the memorial piece is not perfect?

I don't think so, because like I was saying, it's not really about it being perfect. It's just about that feeling. I don't know how to explain it better. It's just this tightness, you know? Like when you're waiting for a pot of water to boil and you turn your back for one second and it boils over. I ruined a really good saucepan that way once. It was this copper-bottom one I got at a thrift store. I love thrift shopping, you can find the most amazing things if you just have the patience to dig. I found this incredible vintage silk scarf last month that had these hand-painted peacocks on it. The colors were so vibrant, like emerald greens and deep sapphire blues. I actually tried to use those exact colors in a painting a few years ago, but I couldn't get the mix right. The blue kept turning out muddy. My art professor in college used to say that mixing the perfect blue was the hardest thing a painter could do. He was this really eccentric guy who always wore a beret, like unironically. He claimed he once lived in a cave in France for a month just to study the shadows...

Ugh, sorry. My brain is doing the thing again. I'm sorry. But yeah, accepting it's not perfect wouldn't help, because I'm not really trying to make it perfect in the first place. I just need that feeling to go away.
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and nudge the objects if you didn't have the fear of dishonoring your aunt's memory?

If I didn't have that fear? Honestly, probably not. I mean, that's actually the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. When I was working on her memorial piece, I just kept getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like, my brain kept telling me that one wrong photo placement or the wrong color choice would mean I didn't love her enough. 

Speaking of color choices, my aunt had this absolute favorite shade of yellow. Like a really soft, buttery yellow. She had her whole kitchen painted that color, and it always smelled like lemon Pledge and fresh coffee in there. She used to buy those flavored coffee beans, the hazelnut ones, from this little local roaster down the street from her house. I tried to go there last month to get some for myself, just for the nostalgia, but the shop actually closed down and got replaced by one of those trendy succulent plant stores. I really don't get the obsession with succulents, honestly. People say they're impossible to kill, but I managed to kill a cactus once. I think I overwatered it? It just sort of... melted into this sad green mush. It was so gross. I had it sitting in this beautiful little ceramic pot that I threw on the wheel back in my undergrad ceramics class...

Ugh, wow, sorry. Tangent again. My brain is just... yeah. I'm sorry. 

But what I meant was, normal creative doubts I can usually just brush off, you know? Like, if a composition is a little heavy on the left, I can just fix it or ignore it. But I couldn't just brush off those thoughts about dishonoring her like normal creative doubts. They felt so heavy. So if those thoughts weren't there... no, I don't think I'd be stuck doing all that checking.
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and nudge the objects if you were certain that your aunt would be honored by the memorial piece, regardless of any small mistakes?

I mean, if I was absolutely certain she'd be honored no matter what? Yeah, I guess that would probably stop the whole checking thing. If I knew for a fact that she wouldn't care about a crooked photo or a weird font choice, I wouldn't have that horrible feeling pushing me to fix it. 

She actually had terrible handwriting herself, now that I think about it. Like, completely illegible. We used to joke that she should have been a doctor because her grocery lists looked like prescriptions. I found one of her old recipe cards the other day when I was looking for her snickerdoodle recipe. Snickerdoodles are my absolute favorite cookie, but only if they're soft in the middle. My roommate in college used to bake them until they were basically hockey pucks. She was a pre-med student, actually, which is funny considering the doctor joke. She studied all hours of the night and drank so much energy drinks I thought her heart was going to explode. She used to leave the empty cans lined up on the windowsill like some kind of weird aluminum trophy collection. The sun would hit them in the morning and wake me up because the glare was so bright...

Sorry. I'm doing it again. But yeah, if I knew she'd be honored regardless, I think the nudging and checking would stop. It's just that I can't ever be 100% certain, you know?
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and nudge the objects if you were able to accept that everyone makes mistakes and it's okay if the memorial piece isn't flawless?

I don't think accepting that everyone makes mistakes would really fix it, because like I said, it's not really about it being flawless. It's more about that feeling of things not being settled. Like, even if I tell myself it's okay if it's not perfect, I still end up rereading the label text a dozen times, or nudging the exact same objects on the display table a fraction of an inch to the left, and then back to the right. I'll just keep checking the layout photos over and over again until my brain finally decides it feels 'settled.' 

And the worst part is, I know it's fine. Like, logically, I know it's already fine, and I'm just completely wasting my studio time. Studio time is so precious, too. I share a space with three other artists, and we all have to coordinate our schedules so we're not stepping on each other's toes. One of them is a sculptor who works with this really intense epoxy resin, and the fumes are just... wow. You have to wear a respirator when she's pouring it. It smells like a mix of nail polish remover and burning plastic. It actually reminds me of this time in high school when my friend Sarah tried to bleach her own hair in my bathroom. She left the bleach on way too long and her hair literally started smoking. It was terrifying, but also kind of hilarious in retrospect. We had to cut off like four inches of her hair, and she ended up wearing beanies for the rest of the semester. She had this one beanie that was neon orange, like a traffic cone...

Sorry. I'm doing it again. But yeah, accepting mistakes wouldn't stop the nudging and the checking the photos. It's just about getting that 'settled' feeling so I can finally stop and get back to work.
Do you think you would still feel the need to check and nudge the objects if you could accept that the memorial piece is good enough as it is?

Honestly, even if I accepted it was good enough, I think I'd still be stuck doing it. It's exactly like I was just saying a minute ago—I can know in my head that it's perfectly fine, that it's good enough as it is, but I'll still end up rereading that label text and nudging the exact same objects on the table back and forth. I'll just keep checking those layout photos over and over until I finally get that 'settled' feeling. It's so frustrating because a big part of me knows it's already fine, and I'm just losing my studio time. 

Which, speaking of time, I actually need to pick up a new wall clock for the studio. The one we have has this incredibly loud ticking sound. Tick, tick, tick, every single second. It drives my studio mate absolutely crazy. She actually took the batteries out of it last Tuesday so we wouldn't have to hear it anymore. She's the one who works with the resin I was telling you about. She also makes these little resin keychains with dried flowers in them. I tried drying flowers once, pressing them inside this massive dictionary I got at a thrift store. The dictionary was from like, 1982, and it smelled like old paper and dust. I love the smell of old books, don't you? There's this used bookstore downtown that has a whole basement full of them, and they have a resident cat named Barnaby who just sleeps on the romance novels all day...

Ugh, sorry. I completely lost my train of thought again. I really am sorry. But yeah, knowing it's good enough doesn't stop the checking and the nudging. I just have to wait for that feeling to settle.

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because when I was working on my aunt’s memorial piece, I kept getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow—like one wrong photo placement or color choice would mean I didn’t love her enough—and I couldn’t just brush them off like normal creative doubts.

I'm an artist, I actually got my degree in illustration, so my family usually asks me to handle the creative stuff for things like this. But anyway, while I was working on her piece, I just kept getting these thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. I don't think accepting that everyone makes mistakes would really fix it, because like I said, it's not really about it being flawless. It's more about that feeling of things not being settled. I'll just keep checking the layout photos over and over again until my brain finally decides it feels 'settled.' 

And the worst part is, I know it's fine. Like, logically, I know it's already fine, and I'm just completely wasting my studio time. Studio time is so precious, too. One of them is a sculptor who works with this really intense epoxy resin, and the fumes are just... wow. You have to wear a respirator when she's pouring it. She left the bleach on way too long and her hair literally started smoking. It was terrifying, but also kind of hilarious in retrospect. We had to cut off like four inches of her hair, and she ended up wearing beanies for the rest of the semester. She had this one beanie that was neon orange, like a traffic cone...

Sorry. I'm doing it again. But yeah, accepting mistakes wouldn't stop the nudging and the checking the photos. It's just about getting that 'settled' feeling so I can finally stop and get back to work.
